result:
There's a specific kind of quiet that only exists at 5:47 in the morning.

It's not the quiet of midnight, which is heavy and performative, a quiet that knows it's supposed to be quiet. Midnight wants to be noticed. It holds its breath. The quiet at 5:47 is different. It's unintentional. The world hasn't woken up yet enough to be loud, but it's no longer asleep enough to be truly still. The refrigerator hums. A bird tries a note and then thinks better of it. Somewhere far off, a truck shifts gears. It's the sound of the world in between, and if you are awake for it — because you woke early, or because you never really slept — you get to hear the house settle into itself.

I think about that in-between a lot. We live most of our lives in the in-betweens and we pretend we don't.

We talk about our lives as if they are made of milestones: birth, graduation, first job, marriage, moving, loss, achievement. We draw our biographies like a connect-the-dots puzzle with big, dark dots. But the actual texture of a life isn't in the dots at all. It's in the lines between them. It's in the three thousand Tuesday afternoons where nothing happened except that you made tea and looked out the window while the kettle boiled. It's in the way you learned to fold your laundry efficiently because your apartment was small. It's in the song that got stuck in your head for an entire summer in 2014 and now, whenever you hear it in a grocery store, you are instantly 23 again.

We are taught to want a story with a climax. But most of us get a life that is much more like a long, meandering river with a lot of interesting stones along the bank.

One of those stones, for me, is the idea of unfinished things.

I keep a mental library of unfinished things. Not failures, not abandoned projects exactly, but things that were left intentionally open. A half-read book that I loved too much to finish because I didn't want it to be over. A sweater I started knitting for a friend who moved away before I could give it to her, so it sits in a drawer, one sleeve perfect and the other still a tangle of yarn. A language I learned enough of to order coffee and ask for directions, but not enough to understand poetry. A friendship that didn't end badly, it just... thinned with distance, like a river spreading into a delta, until checking in once a year felt both too much and not enough.

We tend to treat unfinished as a synonym for incomplete, and incomplete as a synonym for broken. But some things are meant to stay unfinished. They are not puzzles missing a piece; they are doors left ajar so the air can move through.

Consider the way we learn. Real learning is almost entirely unfinished. You never truly finish learning to cook, or to be kind, or to play the guitar, or to be a decent partner or parent or friend. You just get further along. The moment you think you have finished learning something is usually the exact moment you have stopped paying attention to it. The master knows that mastery is not a certificate you hang on the wall. It's a practice. The potter who has thrown ten thousand bowls still centers the clay each morning like it's the first time, because in a very real way, it is.

There is a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi*, which is often simplified as finding beauty in imperfection, but it's more precise than that. It's the beauty of impermanence and incompleteness. A chipped bowl that has been repaired with gold — *kintsugi* — is more beautiful than it was when it was whole, not despite the crack but because the crack is now part of its history. The repair doesn't hide that the bowl was broken. It honors that it was broken and continues to be useful anyway. I think people are like that. We want to present ourselves as unchipped, uncracked, finished products. But the gold seams are where the light actually catches.

The world we have built in the last twenty years does not like the unfinished. The internet wants everything to be searchable, taggable, finalized, archived. We are pressured to have a personal brand, an elevator pitch, a neat narrative arc we can deliver at a dinner party when someone asks, "So what do you do?" We curate our photos down to the nine best squares on a grid. We turn our thoughts into posts that need to have a conclusion, a takeaway, a call to action. Even our casual messages want to be concluded with a little double-checkmark that says *read, resolved, done*.

But analog things resist this. Analog things understand unfinishedness.

A vinyl record has a soft crackle before the music starts, and you can hear the room where it was recorded. A film photograph has grain and a slightly missed focus and a thumb in the corner. A handwritten letter has a place where you crossed something out and wrote it again, and the person reading it can see you thinking in real time. A paper map has a fold line right through the middle of an important town, and you have to unfold it with both hands, and it never quite folds back the same way. These things are inefficient and perfect because of it. They require you to meet them halfway.

I worry sometimes that we are losing our tolerance for halfway. We want instant answers, not the slow process of looking something up in an encyclopedia and getting distracted by the entry next to it. We want our food delivered in thirty minutes, not the three-hour ritual of cooking with someone you love, where the conversation is the point and the food is just the excuse. We want our relationships to be frictionless, but friction is how you know two real surfaces are touching.

Speaking of surfaces, let’s talk about the ocean for a while.

If you want to feel properly unfinished, go stand next to the ocean. Not the pretty, postcard ocean with turquoise water and a perfect sunset, but any ocean. Any cold, gray, indifferent ocean on a Tuesday in November. Stand there and watch it. The ocean does not care about you at all, and that is a profound relief. It was here 300 million years before you were born and it will be here long after the last human light goes out. And yet, for some reason, the salt in your blood is almost exactly as salty as the sea. We carry a little piece of the ocean inside us. Our tears and our sweat are echoes of an ancient shoreline. Every vertebrate that walks on land still brings the sea with it, internally. We left the ocean, but we never really left.

The tide comes in and goes out every day with a logic that has nothing to do with our schedules. It erases footprints and sandcastles with total impartiality. Children understand this intuitively. They will spend four hours building something incredibly elaborate right at the edge of the surf, knowing full well that it will be destroyed. They don't build it despite its impermanence; they build it *because* of it. The joy is in the building. Adults forget this and start building things only if they think they will last forever. We want monuments. Children want games. Games are better.

I was reading recently about deep sea creatures, animals that live so far down that sunlight never reaches them. They make their own light. Bioluminescence. Tiny anglerfish and comb jellies and vampire squid drifting in absolute blackness, lighting themselves up like lanterns. At those depths, the pressure would crush a submarine. It is cold and empty and utterly alien. And yet, it is teeming with life that has solved the problem of darkness not by escaping it, but by becoming luminous inside it. I think about that when I feel low. Not in a forced inspirational poster way, but as a biological fact: there are creatures whose entire evolutionary strategy is to glow in the dark. They don't wait for the sun to come back.

Cities do the same thing, in a different way. A city at night from an airplane window looks exactly like a colony of bioluminescent organisms. We are the things that light ourselves up.

A city is also a great unfinished object. No city is ever finished. Even the most ancient ones — Rome, Istanbul, Jerusalem — are constantly being dug up, patched, rewired, repainted. A city is a palimpsest, a manuscript that has been written on, scraped off, and written on again. You can see it in the layers: a Roman column holding up a medieval wall that has a neon sign bolted to it advertising noodles. In my own city, there is a building that was a bank, then a department store, then an abandoned shell for ten years, and now it's a library. The vault is still in the basement and the kids have story time in it. I love that. We think of history as something that happened, but it's also something that *happens*, continuously, in the bricks.

And the people who live in cities — we write on each other, too. You leave a mark on every place you live, and it leaves a mark on you. You pick up an accent, a way of crossing the street, a favorite corner store, a shortcut through an alley that only locals know. Years after you move away, you will still dream about that apartment with the weird layout where the bathroom door opened directly into the kitchen. Places stay in us like that.

There is a concept in architecture called "desire paths." Those are the unofficial trails that people make when they ignore the paved sidewalk and cut across the grass where they actually want to walk. From above, you can see them: pale lines through the lawn, evidence of collective choice. Planners can lay down the most logical, efficient sidewalks they can imagine, but people will always make desire paths. They show what we really want, not what we were told to want. I think our lives have desire paths, too. The official path says: go to college, get a job, get promoted, buy a house, optimize. But the real, worn grass shows where we actually walked when no one was watching: the hobby we kept for no money, the person we loved that didn't make sense on paper, the three months we spent just reading after a loss because we couldn't do anything else. Follow the desire paths when you can. They know something.

The future, everyone says, is going to be automated, optimized, generated. And it will be, partly. Machines will write and draw and drive and diagnose. And that is incredible and terrifying in equal measure. But I suspect — I hope — that the most human parts of the future will be stubbornly, beautifully handmade.

People will still want to knead bread by hand even when a machine can make a perfect loaf. They will still want to learn to play the piano even though a computer can play it flawlessly. They will still want to plant tomatoes that grow crooked, to mend a shirt, to write a clumsy love letter. Because perfection is not the point. The point is the doing. The point is the way your hands learn something your brain can't articulate. The point is the small, controlled way we push back against entropy for a little while.

Entropy, of course, always wins in the end. Everything you build will eventually fall down. Every book will eventually turn to dust. The sun will eventually expand and swallow the earth. This sounds depressing if you think your job is to make things that last forever. It is liberating if you understand your job is to make things that matter for now.

A good meal matters for now. A kind word to a stranger matters for now. Sitting on the floor and playing with a dog matters for now. You don't need to be eternal to be meaningful. In fact, the brevity is what makes it meaningful. A song is beautiful because it ends. If it went on forever, it would just be noise.

So if you have a drawer full of unfinished things, I would say: let them be unfinished for a little longer. Don't rush to conclude everything. Leave a few doors ajar. Let the air move through.

Go for a walk without a destination. Not for exercise, not to hit ten thousand steps, but just to see what’s there. Look at how the light falls on the side of a building at 4 p.m. Notice the way someone has planted flowers in a discarded bathtub on their porch. Listen to a conversation fragment as you pass strangers. Let your mind wander without demanding it produce anything useful.

Read a book slowly, even if you don't finish it. Start something you might be bad at. Call someone you haven't talked to in a while with no agenda other than to hear their voice. Keep a notebook where you write down small, useless beauties: the exact blue of the sky after a storm, a good sentence you overheard, the way your cat sleeps with one paw over her eyes.

The world will keep trying to convince you that you need to be faster, more finished, more polished, more certain. You don't.

You are allowed to be a work in progress. You are allowed to glow in the dark for a while before anyone sees you. You are allowed to be the river, not just the dots.

And at 5:47 tomorrow morning, when the quiet comes again, you might be awake for it. You might hear the refrigerator hum and the first uncertain bird and know, in that in-between, that being alive is not a problem to be solved. It is a thing to be tended, like a garden, like a sourdough starter, like a half-knit sweater that will keep someone warm one day, even if you don't yet know who.

Let it be unfinished. That is how it stays alive.
